title: A star exploded 440 million years ago—and NASA just found its secret engine!
summary:
When a huge star runs out of fuel, it can collapse and explode in a supernova—one of the brightest events in the universe. But some supernovae are extra bright, shining 10 times more than usual! Scientists call these "superluminous supernovae," and they've been a mystery for 20 years. What gives them that extra kick?

Thanks to NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, we finally have a big clue. Fermi detected powerful gamma rays (the most energetic form of light) coming from a supernova named SN 2017egm, which exploded in a galaxy 440 million light-years away. That's super far, but it's actually one of the closest superluminous supernovae ever seen! By studying these gamma rays, scientists think the hidden engine is a magnetar.

A magnetar is a type of neutron star—the leftover core after a star collapses. But a magnetar has a magnetic field so strong it's hard to imagine: about 10 trillion times stronger than a fridge magnet! This newborn magnetar spins hundreds of times per second, whipping up a storm of particles and energy. That energy gets trapped inside the expanding debris, making the supernova shine extra bright. After a few months, some of the gamma rays finally leak out, and that's what Fermi spotted.

"Only SN 2017egm shows evidence for gamma rays," said researcher Guillem Martí-Devesa. "This opens up a new window for studying these fascinating events." The team tested different models, and the magnetar model fit the data best. They also think future telescopes, like the Cerenkov Telescope Array, could spot similar supernovae even farther away. So next time a star goes boom, we might just catch its hidden engine in action!
why_it_matters: Stars like the one that produced SN 2017egm created many of the elements that make up your body, so studying these explosions helps us understand where our own atoms came from.

keywords.explanation: Superluminous supernovae are star explosions that shine 10 times brighter than normal supernovae and are a big mystery.
A magnetar is a kind of dead star core with a magnetic field so strong it's like trillions of fridge magnets packed together.
A neutron star is the super-dense leftover core after a massive star collapses and goes supernova.
Gamma rays are the most powerful form of light, more energetic than X-rays, and come from the universe's wildest events.
Fermi is a NASA telescope in space that scans the sky for gamma rays coming from black holes, explosions, and other violent things.
A light-year is the distance light travels in one year, used to measure huge spaces between galaxies.

background_read: A supernova marks the violent death of a huge star; for a short time, it can outshine an entire galaxy.

Some supernovae are called superluminous because they are far brighter than usual, and scientists have debated for 20 years whether their extra power comes from a magnetar — a newborn neutron star with a magnetic field quadrillions of times stronger than Earth's.

The Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope (a NASA observatory that has been scanning the sky since 2008) caught gamma rays leaking from SN 2017egm, offering the first direct clue that a magnetar engine is at work.
Article_Structure: WHO: Scientists using NASA's Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope, including researcher Guillem Martí-Devesa.
WHAT: They detected powerful gamma rays from the superluminous supernova SN 2017egm, pointing to a magnetar as the hidden energy source.
WHERE: In a galaxy 440 million light-years from Earth.
WHY: To solve the long-standing mystery of what makes some supernovae extra bright and to open a new window for studying cosmic explosions.

perspectives.description: Detecting gamma rays from a distant supernova finally confirms that magnetars can power these extreme blasts, giving astronomers a new tool to study the universe.

perspectives.perspective: Critical – Just one example so far
perspectives.description: Only SN 2017egm has shown gamma-ray evidence; until we find more, we can't be sure all superluminous supernovae work the same way.
The team tested different ideas and the magnetar model fit best, but other explanations like a black hole engine could still play a role in some cases.
